label: Spain

allocation.label: Proportional by province (D'Hondt), grouped into regions

governmentText.majority: {party} wins {seats} seats, past the 176 line, and is invested at the first ballot with no help from anyone.
governmentText.coalition: {parties} sign a coalition pact worth {seats} seats, enough to win the investiture ballot outright.
governmentText.confidence_supply: {lead} is invested with the votes of {partner}, a deal worth {seats} seats.
governmentText.minority: {party} has {seats} seats and goes to investiture needing rivals to abstain: a simple majority is enough on the second ballot, and the regional parties set the price.
governmentText.hung: No pair of parties reaches 176. {largest} has the most seats, and the King's consultations turn into months of talks with the regional parties before a repeat election looms.

goalHint: Win the most seats and aim for {majority} of {total}. Seats are won province by province, so small regions count and nationalist parties in Catalonia, the Basque Country and the Canaries take seats the national parties need.

issues.name: Jobs & unemployment
issues.blurb: One worker in five out of work, a generation on temporary contracts, and the youth jobless rate above 40%.

issues.name: Austerity & the deficit
issues.blurb: Brussels, the bond markets and the budget cuts that follow.

issues.name: Prices & mortgages
issues.blurb: Food and energy bills, rising interest rates and variable mortgages.

issues.name: Corruption
issues.blurb: Gürtel, the Bárcenas papers and ministers who did not resign.

issues.name: Catalonia & the unity of Spain
issues.blurb: Independence, the referendums, the courts and what Madrid owes the regions.

issues.name: Pensions
issues.blurb: The pension bill, the freeze and who pays for retirement.

issues.name: Housing
issues.blurb: Rents that outrun wages, tourist flats and a generation that cannot leave home.

issues.name: Immigration
issues.blurb: Boats to the Canaries, the border at Ceuta and Melilla and who gets to stay.

issues.name: Health & education
issues.blurb: Waiting lists, regional cuts and the state of the public schools.

issues.name: Political renewal
issues.blurb: The end of two-party politics, new parties and a new way of doing things.

issues.name: Security & ETA
issues.blurb: The end of ETA's violence, its prisoners and the legal return of the Basque left.

blocs.name: Catalan, Basque and Galician identity voters

2011.label: 2011 · Rajoy v. Rubalcaba
2011.tagline: November 2011. Unemployment has passed 21%, the bond markets are punishing Madrid and Zapatero has stepped aside. Rajoy runs a cautious campaign with a huge lead, and Rubalcaba has to carry the government's record. The only question is how large the PP's majority will be.

events.headline: Zapatero brings the election forward and will not stand again. {party} enters the campaign behind a new leader and the worst unemployment in Europe
ETA announces the definitive end of its armed activity. The Basque left has its legal list and {party} says peace is on its side
Borrowing costs climb as the Italian crisis spreads and the bond markets look at Spain. {party} says the numbers prove the government has to go

Rubalcaba and Rajoy meet in the only head-to-head debate, on 7 November. Rubalcaba presses on the cuts, but every snap poll gives the night to Rajoy, and {party} gets a small lift that does not move the vote
Rajoy runs a cautious campaign and refuses to say where the cuts will fall. {party}'s short manifesto draws fire but no real damage
The 15-M indignados say that no party represents them and urge a vote for anyone but the two big parties. {party} and UPyD pick up the anger
Rosa Díez's UPyD, polling at record levels, promises to rewrite the electoral law and reform the regions, and {party} wins over disillusioned voters
Rubalcaba pledges to defend pensions and the public health service, and {party}'s message lands with older voters who have heard these promises before
The PSOE and the PP changed the Constitution in September to cap the deficit, and {party} says the two big parties have already made their deal
Duran i Lleida says the PP is heading for an absolute majority and Catalonia needs CiU as its counterweight in the Cortes, and {party} claims it will be the voice of the Catalan centre
Youth unemployment above 45% lights up the evening news, and {party} is blamed for a generation without work
Galician voters weigh the BNG against the two big parties in a region hit by shipyard and fishing job losses, and {party} claims the local issues

2015.label: 2015 · Rajoy v. Sánchez
2015.tagline: December 2015. Spain is growing again and a fifth of its workforce still has no job. For the first time, four parties can win: Rajoy's PP, Sánchez's PSOE, Iglesias's Podemos and Rivera's Citizens. Break the two-party system, or hold on to it.

events.headline: Rajoy calls the vote for 20 December with Spain growing at 3% and still more than one in five out of work. {party} runs on the recovery and on 'stability'
Rivera's Citizens, fresh from a strong Catalan result and a run of friendly polls, surges toward second place nationally, and {party} fills the gap in the polls the old parties left behind
Rajoy skips the four-way debate on 7 December and sends his deputy, Soraya Sáenz de Santamaría. {party}'s empty chair becomes the debate's best line
In the head-to-head on 14 December, Sánchez tells Rajoy a prime minister must be decent and that Rajoy is not. {party} gets its best day of the campaign
A teenager punches Rajoy in the face on a walkabout in Pontevedra, a few days from the vote. {party}'s leader walks away unhurt and the footage runs all night
Podemos and its local allies, En Comú Podem, Compromís and En Marea, close the campaign with a packed arena in Valencia and 2,000 more outside. {party} finishes with its best crowds
The Gürtel and Bárcenas papers are back in the papers and on the television, and {party} has to answer for money again
Alberto Garzón's IU runs on its own list after talks with Podemos collapse, and {party} claims it is the real left

Fresh from the Junts pel Sí win in the September Catalan election, ERC under Gabriel Rufián and Democràcia i Llibertat take the independence case to Madrid on separate lists, and {party} says Catalonia will be heard in the Congress
The Catalan pro-independence parties claim a mandate after the September regional election, and {party} promises to hold the line
Both newcomers say the old parties had their chance and fell short, and {party} presents itself as a clean start
The drawdown of the Social Security reserve fund to pay pensions comes up again, and {party} has to reassure its older voters
Polls put the PSOE level with Citizens while Podemos closes in, and {party} spends a week answering whether it can hold second place

2019.label: 2019 · Sánchez v. Casado
2019.tagline: April 2019. The Catalan parties have voted down Sánchez's budget and he has called a spring election. The right has split three ways between the PP, Citizens and a Vox fresh from Andalusia, and the Catalan trial runs in the background. Win the most seats and find a majority.

events.headline: ERC and PDeCAT join the right to vote down the budget. Sánchez answers by calling a general election for 28 April, and {party} takes the field as the party of the minimum wage and the pension rise
Twelve Catalan independence leaders go on trial in the Supreme Court, with Vox as a private prosecutor. {party} makes the trial its campaign
Rivera rules out any deal with Sánchez and promises Citizens will be the opposition's leader. It firms up {party}'s right flank and shuts a door
Two televised debates in two nights, on 22 and 23 April. Rivera goes on the attack and wins the first night in several snap polls, and {party} gets the best of the overnight numbers
Casado warns that a vote for Citizens or Vox is a vote that helps Sánchez, and {party} makes a last push for the tactical vote of the right
PSOE warns that the PP, Citizens and Vox will govern Spain as they now govern Andalusia, and {party} sees its own supporters come home
The PNV, whose votes passed Rajoy's last budget and then helped remove him in the June 2018 censure motion, campaigns as the party that gets results for the Basque Country, and {party} gains
The PP, Citizens and Vox join the same Plaza de Colón rally on the Catalan question, and {party} shares a stage with its rivals and its allies
The minimum wage rises to 900 euros a month, and {party} says it is the proof of what a left government can do
Vox fills halls and bullrings with crowds that the pollsters did not expect, and {party} is the story of the week
Iglesias returns from paternity leave with a rally in Madrid and puts a coalition with the PSOE at the centre of {party}'s pitch
Compromís and Podemos run separately in Valencia and split the left vote, and {party} fights over the same voters
Citizens and the PP govern together in Andalusia with Vox's votes, and {party} struggles to explain where it stands on the far right

2023.label: 2023 · Feijóo v. Sánchez
2023.tagline: July 2023. The PP has swept the May local elections and Sánchez has answered by calling a general election in the middle of the summer. Feijóo needs Vox to reach 176 and Sánchez needs a new left alliance and every nationalist in the Congress. Win the most seats, then count the investiture.

events.headline: The PP sweeps the May local elections and Sánchez calls a general election for 23 July the next morning. The gamble catches {party}'s rivals without lists or a plan
The PP signs coalition deals with Vox in Valencia and Extremadura. Sánchez says this is what Feijóo's government would look like, and {party} has to answer for it
After a week of vetoes, Yolanda Díaz and Podemos agree a joint list at the deadline, with Irene Montero left off it. {party} is a single ticket again
Feijóo promises to 'repeal Sánchez-ism', starting with the Democratic Memory law and the Trans law. It sets {party}'s base alight and worries the centre
Sánchez and Feijóo meet for the only head-to-head debate, on 10 July. Sánchez presses on the pacts with Vox, but most snap polls give the night to Feijóo, and {party} gets a lift

Over two million Spaniards request a postal vote for a July election in the holidays. {party}'s provincial machine, the strongest in the country, sets about getting its older voters to the post office
Pride flags come down from some town halls where the PP governs with Vox, and Vox's regional pacts replace the term gender violence. Moderates drift away from {party}
Hundreds of sentence reductions under the Only Yes Means Yes law keep a mistake alive in the news, and {party} cannot shake it
Variable mortgage payments jump again as interest rates rise, and angry homeowners look for someone to blame, starting with {party}
The PP hammers the pardons and the end of the sedition crime in every speech, and {party} hears it in the provinces
A drought and a heatwave put the climate and Doñana on the front page, and {party} says the government waited too long
Polls show Junts and ERC could decide the next prime minister, and {party} presents itself as the price of a left government
A bad month of unemployment figures leads the news and puts the government on the defensive, and {party} looks to be in trouble
Another record rent rise in Madrid and Barcelona fills the evening news, and voters look to {party}
{party}'s leader takes the televised debate on the overnight numbers
A candidate's old tweets resurface, and {party} spends the day apologising
The talk of the tactical vote spreads through Madrid, and support drifts to {party}
{party}'s leader fumbles a question on a morning radio programme and the clip goes round the country
Business leaders and the national papers line up behind {party}
A viral clip breaks for {party} among first-time voters
A bus tour through the small towns of Castile wins {party} friendly local coverage
A flood or a wildfire puts leadership first, and {party} looks the part
A national network offers {party} a head-to-head debate slot
events.prompt: A prime-time debate is on the table. How do you play it?

choices.text: Accept and go on the attack
choices.resultText: You land blows and take a few. The overnight polls twitch your way.
A steady, on-message night. No gaffes, no fireworks.
You dodge the studio lights. The press calls it an empty chair.

events.headline: Every interview asks {party} the same question: what would you do about Catalonia?
events.prompt: Whatever you say will be played back in Barcelona and in Madrid the same evening. What is the answer?

choices.text: Hold your line on Catalonia and do not move
choices.resultText: Your own voters cheer. The other side of the argument hears a door closing.

choices.text: Offer talks and a new financing deal for the regions
choices.resultText: Moderates on both sides listen. The hard liners call it a surrender.

choices.text: Talk about jobs and change the subject
choices.resultText: Nobody is angry, and nobody is satisfied either.

events.headline: Every interview asks {party} the same question: who would you govern with?
events.prompt: The 176 line is a long way off for everyone. What do you say about the deals you would make?

choices.text: Name your partners and campaign as a bloc
choices.resultText: Clarity reassures your side. The other side calls it a stitch-up.
Nobody is ruled out, and nobody is quite reassured.

choices.text: Rule out the other camp and dare voters to choose
choices.resultText: A bold line. It sharpens the contrast with your rival.

events.headline: {party}'s manifesto team is split on the big tax pledge
events.prompt: The manifesto goes to print on Friday. Which way do you push?

choices.text: Go bold with a defining, risky pledge
choices.resultText: The base roars. The Finance Ministry starts sharpening pencils.

choices.text: Play it safe: no hostages to fortune
Make it a contrast with the rival's costings
choices.resultText: You define them more than yourself, and it lands.
